value.overview: The Red-tailed Hawk is a large, powerful bird of prey and one of the most widespread hawks in the Americas. It is recognized for its broad wings, heavy body, and, in many adults, a distinctive rusty-red tail. The species occupies habitats ranging from deserts and grasslands to forest edges, farmland, and mountains. In Costa Rica, it is represented by resident highland birds as well as occasional or seasonal migrants from farther north.
value.classification: The Red-tailed Hawk belongs to the hawk and eagle family Accipitridae and the genus Buteo. Several regional forms are recognized; birds occurring in Costa Rica are generally associated with the Central American form Buteo jamaicensis costaricensis.
value.identification: This is a bulky hawk with broad, rounded wings and a relatively short, wide tail. Adults often show a reddish tail, although immature birds have brown, barred tails and can be difficult to identify. Typical plumage includes a pale underside, a dark belly band, and dark markings along the leading edges of the wings. Costa Rican birds commonly have rich rufous coloration on the belly and underwing linings, with a dark brown head and shoulders. It frequently soars with its wings slightly raised.
value.rangeHabitat: The Red-tailed Hawk has a broad range across North America, the Caribbean, and parts of Central America. In Costa Rica, it occurs mainly in mountainous and highland regions, where resident birds use open country, pasture, agricultural landscapes, forest edges, and adjacent woodlands. It is less typical of dense lowland rainforest. Suitable areas usually provide elevated perches, open hunting ground, and scattered trees or forest patches for nesting. The Costa Rican population is associated with the local highland form B. j. costaricensis.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in much of Costa Rica, especially the highlands, but the country may also receive occasional or seasonal northbound migrants. Unlike strongly migratory Buteo species, most Red-tailed Hawks are sedentary or move only short distances; some northern birds migrate south through Central America during the nonbreeding season.
value.breeding: Red-tailed Hawks are generally monogamous and often maintain territories for several years. They build large stick nests in tall trees, on cliffs, or on other elevated structures, lining them with softer vegetation. The female usually lays one to three eggs, and both adults defend the nest and care for the young. In Costa Rica, resident highland birds can breed locally, although the timing may vary with elevation, rainfall, and local food availability. Nests are often placed near open hunting areas.
value.dietFeeding: The species is an opportunistic predator that commonly eats small mammals such as rats, mice, squirrels, and rabbits. It may also take birds, reptiles, amphibians, and large insects, and sometimes scavenges carrion. Red-tailed Hawks usually hunt from a high perch or while soaring, watching open ground for movement before descending rapidly. In Costa Rica, pastureland, farmland, road edges, and other open areas can provide important hunting habitat.
value.behavior: Red-tailed Hawks often spend long periods perched quietly on trees, poles, fences, or rocky prominences. They soar on thermals with broad wings and may give a characteristic, harsh descending scream, especially near a territory or nest. Pairs defend breeding areas, while nonbreeding birds are generally solitary. Their flight style is steady and deliberate, and they commonly use rising warm air to travel with little wing movement.

conservation.populationTrend: Increasing or broadly stable at the global scale, with strong populations across much of North America.
